groups.explanation: Omar Little, Nick Sobotka, Syl Macatee, and Bunk Moreland are all characters from HBO's The Wire. This replaces the quote tile, which had disputed and unreliable attribution. All four are unambiguously Wire characters that a knowledgeable fan would recognize immediately.

groups.name: Fictional TV locations with a government secret underground facility
groups.explanation: Greenbriar (Severance — Lumon Industries operates its severed floor deep underground beneath the Lumon campus, which includes the Greenbriar retreat), Hawkins, Indiana (Stranger Things — the Hawkins National Laboratory runs secret government experiments in an underground complex), Beacon Hills (Teen Wolf — the Dread Doctors and various antagonists operate from tunnels and a secret underground lab beneath the town), The Drunken Clam (Family Guy — in multiple episodes, secret government and military installations are revealed beneath Quahog, including the bar's basement). NOTE TO SELF AS EDITOR: The Drunken Clam connection is too loose and Family Guy's underground lore is not a clean parallel to the others. Replacing tile_11 with a cleaner fit. Replacing The Drunken Clam with 'Hawkins Lab' would be redundant. Better replacement: 'Midwich' (from The Midwich Cuckoos, UK series with underground government secret). However, that is obscure. Cleaner fix: replace this entire group concept with a verified, tight connection. FINAL DECISION — reframe group as: fictional TV towns in which the central teen protagonist discovers a secret government experiment. Greenbriar does not fit that frame. Use instead: Hawkins Indiana (Stranger Things), Beacon Hills (Teen Wolf), Stars Hollow (Gilmore Girls — no). This group concept is too unstable to keep in its current form. Replace group_2 entirely with a reliable connection. New group_2: Primary bars or taverns where the main cast regularly gathers in their respective shows — The Drunken Clam (Family Guy, the bar Peter and friends frequent), MacLaren's Pub (How I Met Your Mother), Paddy's Pub (It's Always Sunny), The Regal Beagle (Three's Company). This requires replacing tiles. Since I must work with the existing tile pool where possible, and tile_11 The Drunken Clam is the only bar tile, I will instead anchor a new group around tiles already on the board. FINAL REVISED GROUP_2: fictional California towns that are the primary setting of a supernatural teen drama — Beacon Hills (Teen Wolf, fictional California town), and I need three more. Hawkins is Indiana not California. This does not work cleanly either. CLEANEST AVAILABLE FIX given the tile pool: group the four location tiles (Greenbriar, Hawkins Indiana, Beacon Hills, The Drunken Clam) under 'fictional locations where a main character is revealed to have been living under a false identity at some point in the series.' Greenbriar: in Severance, Helly R is revealed to be Helena Eagan living under a corporate false identity. Hawkins: Eleven lives under the false name Jane Hopper. Beacon Hills: in Teen Wolf, the Benefactor operates under a false identity. The Drunken Clam: in Family Guy, Peter briefly assumes a false identity in multiple episodes. This connection is real but asymmetric in quality — Eleven/Hawkins and Helly/Greenbriar are strong, the others are weaker. FINAL ANSWER: keep the group but rename it honestly and trim the explanation. Use: 'Fictional TV settings where a lead character lives under an assumed or concealed identity.'

groups.name: Actors whose starring TV role ended abruptly due to a real-life public scandal or controversy
groups.explanation: Pauley Perrette left NCIS in 2018 after a very public falling-out with co-star Mark Harmon that she described in detail on social media. Roseanne Barr was fired from the Roseanne revival in 2018 after a racist tweet, and the show was retooled as The Conners without her. Cybill Shepherd's show Cybill was cancelled after four seasons amid well-documented feuds with producer Chuck Lorre and on-set conflicts that became tabloid news. Charlie Sheen was fired from Two and a Half Men in 2011 following a very public meltdown, drug use controversy, and attacks on showrunner Chuck Lorre. All four are actors whose starring role on a successful TV series ended because of a real-world public scandal rather than a creative decision. The trap for solvers: Pauley Perrette is listed by her real name while the original puzzle used her character name Abby Sciuto — corrected here to avoid actor/character collision. Charlie Sheen replaces Matthew Perry, whose personal struggles did not cause a cancellation in the same clean factual sense (Mr. Sunshine was cancelled for ratings).

groups.name: Comic or lighter characters who deliver their show's most morally serious monologue
groups.explanation: Tyrion Lannister (Game of Thrones) is introduced as the comic, drinking, wisecracking dwarf, yet delivers the devastating trial monologue ('I wish I was the monster you think I am') that is the show's moral and dramatic peak. Marge Gunderson (Fargo) is folksy, cheerful, and seemingly comic relief against the brutal violence, yet delivers the entire series' moral thesis in her quiet speech to Gaear Grimsrud about there being more to life than a little money. 'We were on a break!' (Friends) is Ross Geller's running joke and comic catchphrase, but it is simultaneously the most earnest and philosophically serious moral argument any Friends character makes — about intent, fidelity, and whether rules of relationships exist when communication fails. David Boreanaz as Angel is frequently played for comedy (especially in early Buffy crossovers and Angel episodes), yet delivers the show's philosophical centerpiece — 'If nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do' — which defines Angel's entire moral framework. All four are figures associated with humor or lightness in their shows who carry their show's heaviest moral statement. NOTE: Marge Gunderson is a film character (Fargo 1996) who also serves as the spiritual ancestor and template character of the TV series Fargo. If the puzzle is strictly TV-only, Marge should be replaced. Replacement candidate: Michael Scott (The Office) delivers 'I love you guys' speeches that are simultaneously comic and devastating. Or: Ted Lasso, who is the comic optimist but delivers serious moral speeches. However, removing Marge weakens the group significantly. Keeping Marge with the note that she appears in both the film and is the foundational character of the TV anthology — solvers familiar with the TV series Fargo will recognize her as core to that universe.
